## TL;DR

Review round 1 identified several ways the new HTTPS discovery path could still report machines as unreachable or misrepresent their projects. I updated the shared discovery flow and its server and Hub consumers: peers are probed on RepoOS's supported Tailscale Serve ports, valid versioned endpoint responses preserve per-project URLs and metadata, and malformed or unrelated service responses still reach the SSH fallback. The Hub now reconciles failures against saved machine hosts and only shows its empty state when there are no projects or failures. Discovery-off and peer access checks are enforced by the peer endpoint. The required changed-path check passed after formatting.

## Work and rationale

The review's main functional issue was that the first HTTP implementation treated a machine as one origin on implicit port 443. RepoOS already configures Tailscale HTTPS Serve on 443, 8443, and 10000, so a peer on another supported port would not answer. I exported the existing port list from `src/core/tailscale.ts` and reused it in the shared core discovery implementation to keep the candidate set aligned with Serve configuration. Each HTTPS and HTTP candidate is probed concurrently with a three-second per-request budget. This gives TLS and Serve time to answer without adding a serial delay per port, and keeps peer work bounded by the existing whole-pass deadline.

The new peer endpoint returns each valid registry entry with its own project name, port, root, allowlist group, validity, and mapped Serve URL. The URL comes from that machine's `tailscale serve status --json` mapping for the registry port, not the incoming request's Host header. That preserves multiple projects on one machine when their Serve ports differ, and keeps the row shape useful to allowlist-group propagation. The payload carries a discovery version. Core accepts only the known version, including its explicit disabled response; invalid JSON, arbitrary JSON, or an older peer response falls through to SSH. This avoids interpreting another service on a candidate port as a successful empty RepoOS result.

The mobile merge logic now checks an unreachable row's host, DNS name, or display name against saved server hostnames. A match is represented as saved with an “Already saved” note and is excluded from the failure group. For reachable rows the existing normalized-origin matching still applies. I also changed the Hub's empty-state paragraph to use an independent condition: it appears only when there are no projects, no failures, and no message or error. The failures details remains collapsed and now has its own visual styles.

Peer filtering now examines both HostName and DNSName and includes device-model patterns such as “Nothing Phone (3a)” even when Tailscale provides no mobile OS value. It retains OS and tag filtering, while avoiding the previous generic `phone` match that could exclude a server called `phone-01`.

The peer endpoint enforces `tailnetDiscovery === false` itself and returns a versioned disabled result before reading the registry. It no longer trusts `X-Forwarded-For`. Direct requests must originate from a Tailnet address. Tailscale Serve's loopback proxy is accepted only when it supplies its injected `Tailscale-User-Login` identity header. The endpoint is an exact public path so a peer can call it without a RepoOS session, while all access still passes through this endpoint gate.

## Approaches tried

I reused the port configuration already owned by `tailscale.ts` instead of maintaining another list in the discovery module. I preserved the SSH path as a compatibility fallback instead of treating all reachable HTTP services as RepoOS. The response version marker lets an explicit disabled server be distinguished from an old or unrelated server without suppressing fallback. Per-project URLs are taken from local Serve mappings by project port, rather than deriving them from the request authority.

## Challenges and blockers

The initial UI build caught TypeScript narrowing issues in safe JSON parsing and an inferred empty-object type for the optional URL map; both were corrected before the final check. The first scoped check also caught formatter differences in four edited files. I ran the repository formatter and repeated the exact required command. The review report's requested endpoint security fix depends on Tailscale Serve's identity header for its loopback listener; this work has automated validation but no live tailnet or physical-phone exercise, so it does not claim those external checks were observed.

## Key learnings

Tailnet discovery crosses several contracts at once: the CLI and Hub share core collection, machine-level Serve can front multiple project ports, and discovered rows also feed allowlist group propagation. Keeping the peer payload aligned with the SSH row shape avoids regressions outside the Hub. A versioned endpoint is important because a successful HTTP status alone does not prove RepoOS answered. Finally, saved-state reconciliation needs machine identity as well as project URL identity: a failed probe has no discovered origin, but its host can still match a server the user already saved.
